category.name: App Security
category.description: Application-layer threat modeling: authentication, sessions, data handling and third-party integrations.

lab.title: E-Commerce Checkout
lab.summary: Analyze a checkout flow that processes user accounts, payments, and order data.
lab.businessContext: A retail company is launching a checkout flow for authenticated customers. Card data is handled by a third-party processor, but the platform stores order history, addresses, and partial card metadata.
lab.systemContext: A browser client talks to a Next.js storefront, which calls an internal orders API. The API reads and writes an orders database, caches sessions in Redis, and calls an external payment processor. Fulfilment events are published to a queue consumed by a warehouse service.

nodes.label: Customer
nodes.description: Authenticated shopper completing a purchase in a browser.

nodes.label: Storefront Web
nodes.description: Server-rendered storefront. Terminates the user session and proxies checkout calls to the orders API.

nodes.label: Orders API
nodes.description: Internal service that validates carts, prices orders, and orchestrates payment and fulfilment.

nodes.label: Session Cache
nodes.description: Redis instance holding session records and cart state. No TLS configured on the internal link.

nodes.label: Orders Database
nodes.description: PostgreSQL store for orders, addresses, and the last four digits of the card used.

nodes.label: Payment Processor
nodes.description: External PCI-compliant processor. Receives card data and returns an authorization token plus asynchronous webhooks.

nodes.label: Fulfilment Queue
nodes.description: Message queue carrying paid-order events to the warehouse. Messages include full shipping addresses.

nodes.label: Warehouse Service
nodes.description: Consumes fulfilment events and triggers physical shipment. Operated by a logistics vendor inside the network perimeter.

trustBoundaries.label: Internet
trustBoundaries.description: Untrusted public network and third parties outside the company perimeter.

trustBoundaries.label: Public DMZ
trustBoundaries.description: Internet-facing tier that terminates TLS and holds user sessions.

trustBoundaries.label: Private Network
trustBoundaries.description: Internal services and data stores not directly reachable from the internet.

architectureIssues.title: Session store holds plaintext session data
architectureIssues.description: The storefront writes session material to a Redis-style cache over an unencrypted protocol and the cache itself applies no encryption at rest. Anything able to read that cache can impersonate a signed-in customer.
architectureIssues.hint: Look at the protocol label on the flow into the cache.

architectureIssues.title: Internal traffic between web tier and API is unencrypted
architectureIssues.description: The storefront calls the orders API over plain HTTP while crossing from the public DMZ into the private network. A trust boundary is crossed without transport protection.
architectureIssues.hint: Compare the protocol on this flow with the one used to reach the database.

architectureIssues.title: Payment webhook has no stated authentication
architectureIssues.description: The payment processor calls back into the orders API. Nothing in the design describes signature verification or replay protection on that inbound callback.
architectureIssues.hint: Who else on the internet can reach that callback endpoint?

architectureIssues.title: Fulfilment queue has no consumer authorization
architectureIssues.description: Paid-order events carrying customer addresses flow to a queue consumed by the warehouse service with no described authentication between the queue and its consumers.
architectureIssues.hint: What stops another service from subscribing to this topic?

architectureIssues.title: Order database concentrates customer PII
architectureIssues.description: Addresses, contact details and partial card metadata all sit in one database with no described field-level protection or retention limit.
architectureIssues.hint: Think about blast radius if a single credential leaks.

architectureIssues.title: No rate limiting on the checkout entry point
architectureIssues.description: Nothing in the architecture describes throttling on the customer-facing checkout flow, leaving both card testing and credential stuffing unbounded.
architectureIssues.hint: What stops an attacker from trying thousands of cards?

threats.title: Session hijacking via unencrypted session cache
threats.description: An attacker with read access to the session cache — through a misconfiguration, a shared network segment, or a compromised neighbouring service — can lift a live session identifier and act as that customer without ever seeing their password.
threats.learnerExplanation: Sessions are bearer credentials. Anything that can read them can become the user.

threats.title: Man-in-the-middle on the DMZ to private network hop
threats.description: The plain HTTP call from the storefront to the orders API crosses a trust boundary. An attacker positioned on that segment can read order contents and tamper with prices or quantities in flight.
acceptedAliases: tampering with order data in transit
threats.learnerExplanation: A trust boundary crossing without transport security is an interception point.

threats.title: Forged payment confirmation webhook
threats.description: Without signature verification an attacker can POST a fake 'payment succeeded' callback to the orders API, causing goods to ship for an order that was never paid for.
threats.learnerExplanation: An inbound callback from a third party is untrusted input until proven otherwise.

threats.title: Bulk disclosure of customer PII from the order database
threats.description: A single compromised credential or an injection flaw in the orders API exposes every stored address, contact detail and partial card record at once.
threats.learnerExplanation: Concentrated personal data raises the cost of any single failure.

threats.title: Card testing through the unthrottled checkout
threats.description: An attacker drives stolen card numbers through checkout to discover which are live. The retailer absorbs the processor fees and risks losing its merchant standing.
threats.learnerExplanation: Fraud abuse is a threat even when no data is disclosed.

threats.title: Unauthorized consumption or injection on the fulfilment queue
threats.description: With no consumer authentication, an attacker who reaches the queue can read customer shipping addresses or inject fabricated fulfilment events to have goods dispatched.
threats.learnerExplanation: Message infrastructure needs the same authorization discipline as an API.

threats.title: Insufficient audit trail for order and payment changes
threats.description: No described logging of who changed an order or when a payment state transitioned, so a disputed or fraudulent transaction cannot be reconstructed afterwards.
threats.learnerExplanation: Repudiation is the quietest STRIDE category and the easiest to forget.

mitigations.title: Encrypt session store and require authenticated TLS to it
mitigations.description: Terminate TLS on the cache, require credentials, and encrypt session payloads at rest so a read of the store yields nothing usable.

mitigations.title: Mutual TLS between the web tier and internal services
mitigations.description: Require mTLS on every trust boundary crossing so internal hops are both encrypted and mutually authenticated.

mitigations.title: Verify webhook signatures and reject replays
mitigations.description: Validate the processor's HMAC signature over the raw body, enforce a timestamp window, and reject duplicate event identifiers.

mitigations.title: Field-level encryption plus retention limits on customer data
mitigations.description: Encrypt personal fields with a separately managed key, tokenize card metadata, and delete records past their retention window.

mitigations.title: Rate limiting and velocity checks on checkout
mitigations.description: Throttle per account, per IP and per card fingerprint, with escalating friction on repeated failed authorizations.

mitigations.title: Authenticated queue with per-consumer authorization
mitigations.description: Require credentials to publish or subscribe and scope each consumer to only the topics its role needs.

mitigations.title: Append-only audit log for order and payment state changes
mitigations.description: Record actor, action, before and after state to storage the application cannot rewrite.

mitigations.title: Web application firewall in front of the storefront
mitigations.description: A useful perimeter control that blocks common injection and bot patterns, but it does not address any of the design flaws in this system.

threatMitigations.explanation: Removes the plaintext session material an attacker would need to steal.
Encrypts and authenticates the boundary crossing, closing the interception point.
Signature and replay checks mean only the real processor can confirm a payment.
Limits what a single leaked credential yields and shrinks the retained dataset.
Velocity limits make bulk card testing uneconomic.
Only authorized services can publish or consume fulfilment events.
An append-only trail makes disputed transactions reconstructable.

releaseGuidance.rationale: Two critical issues — the plaintext session store and the unauthenticated payment webhook — are exploitable with no privileged position and lead directly to account takeover and unpaid fulfilment. Neither requires a re-architecture; both are contained, well-understood fixes. A defensible position is to hold the launch until those two are closed and to schedule the transport and data-protection work behind them. Arguing for 'do not ship' is also reasonable if the team cannot commit to a date for the webhook fix.
suggestedConditions: Encrypt the session store and require authenticated TLS before public launch.
Verify payment webhook signatures with replay protection before accepting live payments.
Commit to a dated plan for mTLS on the DMZ to private network hop.
Enable checkout rate limiting ahead of the first marketing campaign.
Turn on audit logging for order and payment state transitions.
